<reason>A wins because it controlled the motion's comparative frame from the start and repeatedly turned B's own words into concessions: "changed skylines," "a glut, a bust," and the arguendo "trims prices a few percent" all became evidence that supply lowers prices. A won the filtering-window exchange (a 2007 unit is precisely today's mid-market stock), gave the clearest incumbent-side mechanism (vacancy, renewal letters, redirected bidding), and its point that the 40% national surge is baseline in both worlds was never squarely answered — B5.5 merely restated the zero-effect claim. B fought well: the binding-constraint timeline, the land-repricing answer to A's sprawl question, and the "immunized" charge were real hits, and B executed format cleanly while A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped. But B's route required near-total absorption (a heroically strong claim), B never engaged Minneapolis at all, and B's closing assertion that Miami's cranes "never touched its rents" contradicted B's own "glut, bust" description. On the motion as written — "more affordable," not "affordable" — B conceded the comparative logic too many times while only defending, never establishing, the zero-effect counterfactual.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 response on Miami: B introduced Miami as a counterexample ("a glut, a bust, foreclosed towers"), and A flipped it — a glut is supply exceeding demand and a bust is prices falling, so B's own exhibit showed supply moving prices, while B never supplied Miami's no-build counterfactual. Paired with A's unanswered closing point that the national price surge is baseline in both worlds and cannot decide a comparative motion, this left B defending an unproven zero-effect position.</best_rebuttal>
